lessons.title: Case Study: Re-Backtesting a Popular Strategy With Realistic Costs

children.text: Every case study so far in this course showed a strategy that looked good and turned out to be far worse than advertised. This one runs the full Lesson 2 checklist against one of the most widely shared strategies in retail trading content, the golden cross, and shows something slightly different: not every popular strategy collapses, but you only find that out by actually running the checklist, not by assuming.
The Strategy: The Golden Cross on Nifty 50 Stocks

Buy a stock when its 50-day simple moving average crosses above its 200-day simple moving average, the golden cross. Sell when it crosses back below, the death cross. Applied across Nifty 50 constituents over a 10-year backtest, as commonly presented in retail trading content, no transaction costs, no slippage, fills at the crossover day's own close, and today's Nifty 50 membership list applied across the full 10 years, the naive version of this backtest shows a 16.50% gross CAGR.

stats.label: Estimated turnover

children.text: A crossover is only confirmed once a day's close is final, so the naive backtest's same-day fill is exactly the unrealistic fill flagged in Lesson 1. Correcting to a next-session-open fill costs 1.20 percentage points, smaller than the momentum example in Lesson 1 because a slow 50/200-day crossover reacts to a much more gradual, less abruptly-priced-in change than a sharp breakout signal does.

The naive backtest used today's Nifty 50 constituent list for the full 10-year window, silently excluding stocks that were removed from the index, often after underperforming, before the backtest period ended. Rebuilding the universe using the actual historical constituent list at each point in time costs a further 0.80 percentage points.

At an estimated 1.5x annual turnover and a blended round-trip cost of 0.20%, tighter than the 0.30% used elsewhere in this course because this strategy trades only the most liquid Nifty 50 names, cost drag from Chapters 2 and 3 combined comes to 0.30 percentage points.

body.text: This is a genuinely different outcome from every other case study in this course. A slow-turnover, large-cap trend strategy is simply far less cost-sensitive than a high-frequency scalp or a fast-rotating momentum book, and the golden cross survives realistic treatment with most of its edge intact. That is exactly why the checklist matters even for strategies that feel obviously fine: you cannot know whether a strategy is a Chapter 2 Bank Nifty scalp or a Chapter 5 golden cross until you have actually run the numbers.

children.text: Two things protected this strategy that were missing in this course's other case studies: low turnover, 1.5x a year against 37.5x for the daily rebalance case in Chapter 4, and a liquid-only universe, Nifty 50 rather than midcaps or smallcaps, keeping both spread and market impact small. The corrections here came almost entirely from methodology, fill timing and index membership, not from the cost stack, because a strategy trading this infrequently in this liquid a universe barely notices transaction costs or slippage in the first place.

body.title: Quick Check
body.question: In this case study, which two of the four checklist categories from Lesson 2 accounted for almost the entire 2.30-point correction?
options: Methodology integrity (fill timing and index membership) and turnover/break-even
Fill timing and index membership, both methodology integrity issues; the full cost stack contributed only 0.30 of the 2.30 points
Turnover/break-even alone, since the strategy's low turnover was the only meaningful factor
body.explanation: 1.20 points came from fixing the same-day fill and 0.80 points from fixing index membership, both methodology integrity issues from Lesson 1, a combined 2.00 of the 2.30-point total. The full cost stack, transaction costs plus slippage and impact, added only 0.30 points, because this strategy's low turnover and liquid universe made it naturally cost-light.

body.text: Not every popular strategy collapses under a realistic backtest, and that is precisely why the checklist has to be run on every strategy, not just the ones that feel suspicious. The golden cross lost most of its correction to methodology bugs, not to cost, a genuinely different failure profile from every other case study in this course, and the only way to know that in advance is to actually run the numbers.

points: A naive golden cross backtest on Nifty 50 stocks showed 16.50% gross CAGR; running the full Chapter 5 checklist brought it to a still-respectable 14.20%, a 2.30-point, roughly 14% relative correction.
Methodology fixes, realistic fill timing and historical index membership, accounted for 2.00 of the 2.30-point correction; the full explicit-cost and slippage stack added only 0.30 points.

Low turnover (1.5x annually) and a liquid-only universe (Nifty 50) made this strategy naturally resistant to the cost sensitivity that devastated the high-turnover strategies examined earlier in this course.

The checklist's job is not to prove every strategy is broken, it is to replace assumption with measurement, and in this case the measurement showed a popular strategy was largely as advertised, once methodology was fixed.
